title_en: First Clement: The Letter to the Corinthians
author: Clement of Rome (traditional attribution; the letter itself is anonymous, written from the church of God sojourning in Rome)
addressee: The church of God sojourning in Corinth
occasion: The Roman church writes to Corinth because a few rash and arrogant people have stirred up a disgraceful and unholy faction (στάσις), greatly blaspheming the Corinthians' renowned name. The text later makes clear this faction involved the removal or transfer of certain well-regarded presbyters from their honored ministry.
argument: The letter rebukes the Corinthians for envy and factionalism (ζῆλος, ἔρις, στάσις), which have led them to remove or transfer certain well-regarded presbyters from their honored ministry. It calls them to repentance, humility, and obedience to God's ordered will, using examples from Scripture, nature, and the apostles. The author argues that God has established a fixed order of ministry through Christ and the apostles, and that removing or transferring duly appointed leaders is a grave sin. The Corinthians must restore peace and harmony by submitting to their presbyters and ending the faction.

outline.move: Greeting, praise for Corinth's former virtue, and rebuke for the recent faction.
Examples of envy from Scripture and recent martyrdoms, including Peter and Paul.
Call to repentance, with examples of Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Lot, and Rahab.
Exhortation to humility, modeled on Christ and the saints.
The harmony of creation as a model for the church; warning against doubt.
The resurrection as a ground for hope and holy living.
Blessing comes through faith and good works, not self-justification; Christ is our high priest.

The army and body as models of ordered submission (37-38); the foolishness of human boasting (39); worship and offerings must follow God's appointed order with proper hierarchy of high priest, priests, Levites, and laity (40-41).
The apostles appointed bishops and deacons by God's will; removing or transferring them is a sin.

The suffering of righteous people and God's protection of them (45); call to cling to holy examples and warning against schism with dominical saying about scandalizing the elect (46); specific rebuke of the current schism as worse than the Paul-Cephas-Apollos parties because it involves unapproved men, not apostles (47); call to repentance and restoration of brotherly love (48-50); confession of sins and warning about hard-heartedness like Pharaoh and the rebels against Moses (51).
Repentance, intercession, and examples of self-sacrifice; the faction must submit.
A long prayer for the church and for rulers.
Closing exhortation, commendation of the messengers, and final blessing.

key_terms.sense: Faction, sedition, the divisive uprising in Corinth
Envy or jealousy, the root cause of the Corinthian strife
Elders, the duly appointed leaders of the Corinthian church
Bishops or overseers, appointed by the apostles
Ministry or service, especially the ordered worship and office in the church
Love, especially the bond that unites the church
Rule or standard, especially the fixed order of ministry and tradition
Persons, the few individuals who stirred up the faction

names.ὁ παντεπόπτης: the All-Seeing (epithet for God in section 55)

scripture: The author quotes the Septuagint (LXX) and follows its book names and Psalm numbering. Modern citations should use standard English Bible names and numbering, e.g. LXX Psalm 50 = Psalm 51 in English Bibles. The author also cites non-canonical or now-lost writings as Scripture.
uncertain: The exact date of composition; c. 96 CE is traditional but not certain.
Whether Clement of Rome is the actual author; the letter is anonymous.
The identity of the 'foolish and senseless' people who mock the church in section 39.
The precise source of some quotations attributed to Scripture, which may come from lost apocryphal works.
The exact nature of the 'misfortunes and setbacks' mentioned in section 1.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The text later makes clear this faction involved the removal or transfer of certain well-regarded presbyters from their honored ministry.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text later makes clear this faction involved the removal or transfer of certain well-regarded presbyters from their honored ministry (section 44: 'ὁρῶμεν γάρ, ὅτι ἐνίους ὑμεῖς μετηγάγετε καλῶς πολιτευομένους ἐκ τῆς ἀμέμπτως αὐτοῖς τετιμημένης λειτουργίας').

_unresolved_facts.claim: Clement: Traditional author; the letter itself does not name him and is formally anonymous, written from the church of God sojourning in Rome.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἡ ἐκκλησία τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ παροικοῦσα Ῥώμην...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The name 'Clement' or 'Κλήμης' never appears in the source text. The letter is completely anonymous, written from 'the church of God sojourning in Rome.' No source forms for Clement exist in the text.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὕτως γὰρ εἶπεν: Ἐλεᾶτε, ἵνα ἐλεηθῆτε... (section 13); ὁ κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστός... (section 16); Δεῦτε, τέκνα, ἀκούσατέ μου... (section 22); εἶπεν γάρ: Οὐαὶ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ ἐκείνῳ... (section 46)
_unresolved_facts.fix: Christ: sections [13, 16, 22, 46]. Note: In section 13, the sayings introduced by 'οὕτως γὰρ εἶπεν' are dominical sayings of Jesus. In section 16, Isaiah's suffering servant passage is applied to Christ by the author, not spoken by Christ. In section 22, the quotation from Psalm 34 is attributed to Christ speaking through the Spirit. In section 46, the dominical saying about scandalizing the elect is introduced by 'εἶπεν γάρ'.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οἱ λειτουργοὶ τῆς χάριτος τοῦ θεοῦ διὰ πνεύματος ἁγίου περὶ μετανοίας ἐλάλησαν. (section 8); λέγει γὰρ τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον: (section 13); φησὶν γὰρ ὁ ἅγιος λόγος: (section 16)
_unresolved_facts.fix: Holy Spirit: sections [8, 13]. Note: Section 16 has 'ὁ ἅγιος λόγος' (the holy word), not 'τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον' (the Holy Spirit). The brief incorrectly conflates 'holy word' with 'Holy Spirit' in section 16.

_unresolved_facts.claim: ὁ παντεπόπτης: the All-Seeing (epithet for God in section 55)
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ παντεπόπτης θεὸς καὶ δεσπότης τῶν πνευμάτων καὶ κύριος πάσης σαρκός (section 64)
_unresolved_facts.fix: ὁ παντεπόπτης: the All-Seeing (epithet for God in section 64, not 55)
